blocks.en: Sardis: A Name That You Are Alive, But You Are Dead
blocks.es_reference: Sardis: Tienes Nombre de que Vives, y Estás Muerto

blocks.en: To Sardis the letter comes from "He who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars" (Revelation 3:1) — Christ in the fullness of the Spirit, holding the churches in His hand. His verdict is one of the most sobering in the book: "I know your works, that you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead" (Revelation 3:1). Sardis had a reputation. To those around it, it looked like a living church, busy and respected. But the eyes that search the lampstands saw past the reputation to the truth, that inwardly it was dead. A congregation can keep its name, its buildings, and its routines long after the life has gone out of it — a church that has become, in effect, a morgue, orderly and quiet, yet a place of the dead. The risen Christ does not flatter such a church; He tells it the truth. Yet even here there is hope, for He does not pronounce it dead and leave it there. He calls, "Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die" (Revelation 3:2). Something still remained; the embers were not all cold. They were to wake up, to strengthen what was left, to remember how they had received and heard the gospel, to hold fast, and to repent (Revelation 3:3). And He warns that if they will not watch, He will come upon them like a thief, at an hour they do not expect.
blocks.es_reference: A Sardis la carta viene de "el que tiene los siete Espíritus de Dios, y las siete estrellas" (Apocalipsis 3:1) — Cristo en la plenitud del Espíritu, sosteniendo las iglesias en su mano. Su veredicto es uno de los más solemnes del libro: "Yo conozco tus obras, que tienes nombre de que vives, y estás muerto" (Apocalipsis 3:1). Sardis tenía una reputación. A los que la rodeaban les parecía una iglesia viva, ocupada y respetada. Pero los ojos que escudriñan los candeleros vieron más allá de la reputación hasta la verdad, que por dentro estaba muerta. Una congregación puede conservar su nombre, sus edificios y sus rutinas mucho después de que la vida se le ha ido — una iglesia que se ha convertido, en efecto, en una morgue, ordenada y silenciosa, pero un lugar de los muertos. El Cristo resucitado no adula a tal iglesia; le dice la verdad. Sin embargo, aun aquí hay esperanza, pues no la declara muerta y la deja ahí. Llama: "Sé vigilante, y confirma las otras cosas que están para morir" (Apocalipsis 3:2). Algo aún permanecía; las brasas no estaban del todo frías. Habían de despertar, fortalecer lo que quedaba, recordar cómo habían recibido y oído el evangelio, retenerlo, y arrepentirse (Apocalipsis 3:3). Y advierte que si no velan, vendrá sobre ellos como ladrón, a una hora que no esperan.

blocks.en: Sardis: A Few Names in White
blocks.es_reference: Sardis: Unas Pocas Personas en Vestiduras Blancas

blocks.en: Even in a dying church, the Lord knows every faithful soul. "You have a few names even in Sardis who have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with Me in white, for they are worthy" (Revelation 3:4). The defiled garment pictures a life stained by sin and compromise; the few who had kept themselves clean would walk with Christ in white, the dress of purity and victory. This leads to the promise to the overcomer: "He who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments, and I will not blot out his name from the Book of Life; but I will confess his name before My Father and before His angels" (Revelation 3:5). Three promises are bound together — white garments of righteousness, a name kept secure in the Book of Life, and open acknowledgment by Christ Himself before the Father and the holy angels. The dead church is called to wake; the faithful within it are assured that Christ knows them by name and will own them at the last. The same Lord who exposes what is dead tenderly guards what is alive.
blocks.es_reference: Aun en una iglesia que muere, el Señor conoce a cada alma fiel. "Tienes unas pocas personas en Sardis que no han ensuciado sus vestiduras, y andarán conmigo en vestiduras blancas; porque son dignas" (Apocalipsis 3:4). La vestidura ensuciada retrata una vida manchada por el pecado y la transigencia; los pocos que se habían guardado limpios andarían con Cristo en vestiduras blancas, el vestido de la pureza y la victoria. Esto lleva a la promesa al que vence: "El que venciere será vestido de vestiduras blancas; y no borraré su nombre del libro de la vida, y confesaré su nombre delante de mi Padre, y delante de sus ángeles" (Apocalipsis 3:5). Tres promesas se unen — vestiduras blancas de justicia, un nombre guardado seguro en el libro de la vida, y el reconocimiento abierto por Cristo mismo delante del Padre y de los santos ángeles. La iglesia muerta es llamada a despertar; los fieles dentro de ella tienen la certeza de que Cristo los conoce por nombre y los reconocerá al fin. El mismo Señor que expone lo que está muerto guarda tiernamente lo que está vivo.

blocks.en: Philadelphia: The Open Door
blocks.es_reference: Filadelfia: La Puerta Abierta

blocks.en: To Philadelphia the letter comes from "He who is holy, He who is true, He who has the key of David, He who opens and no one shuts, and shuts and no one opens" (Revelation 3:7). Christ holds the key of David, the authority to open and close the door of the kingdom, and what He opens no power on earth can shut. To this church He says, "I have set before you an open door, and no one can shut it; for you have a little strength, have kept My word, and have not denied My name" (Revelation 3:8). Philadelphia was not a powerful church; it had only "a little strength." Yet it had been faithful in the two things that matter most, for it had kept Christ's word and had not denied His name. To such a faithful, weak church Christ gives not a rebuke but an open door — an opportunity for witness and an entrance into His kingdom that no enemy can close. It is faithfulness, not strength, that He honors, and a small church that holds fast His word lacks nothing it truly needs.
blocks.es_reference: A Filadelfia la carta viene de "el Santo, el Verdadero, el que tiene la llave de David, el que abre y ninguno cierra, y cierra y ninguno abre" (Apocalipsis 3:7). Cristo tiene la llave de David, la autoridad para abrir y cerrar la puerta del reino, y lo que él abre ningún poder en la tierra puede cerrarlo. A esta iglesia le dice: "He dado una puerta abierta delante de ti, y ninguno la puede cerrar; porque tienes un poco de fuerza, y has guardado mi palabra, y no has negado mi nombre" (Apocalipsis 3:8). Filadelfia no era una iglesia poderosa; tenía solo "un poco de fuerza." Sin embargo, había sido fiel en las dos cosas que más importan, pues había guardado la palabra de Cristo y no había negado su nombre. A tal iglesia fiel y débil Cristo le da no una reprensión sino una puerta abierta — una oportunidad para el testimonio y una entrada a su reino que ningún enemigo puede cerrar. Es la fidelidad, no la fuerza, lo que él honra, y una iglesia pequeña que retiene su palabra no carece de nada que verdaderamente necesite.

blocks.en: Philadelphia: Kept Through the Hour of Trial
blocks.es_reference: Filadelfia: Guardada de la Hora de la Prueba

blocks.en: Christ promises to vindicate Philadelphia before its enemies, making those of "the synagogue of Satan" come and bow at their feet and know that He has loved them (Revelation 3:9). Then comes a precious promise: "Because you have kept My command to persevere, I also will keep you from the hour of trial which shall come upon the whole world" (Revelation 3:10). Christians have understood "keep you from the hour of trial" in more than one way — some as being kept safe through the trial, others as being kept out of it altogether — and the course leaves that question open, noting only the certainty that Christ will keep His faithful people. He adds, "Behold, I am coming quickly! Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown" (Revelation 3:11). To the overcomer He promises to make him "a pillar in the temple of My God," permanent and secure, inscribed with the name of God, the name of the city of God, the New Jerusalem, and Christ's own new name (Revelation 3:12). Like Smyrna, Philadelphia receives no rebuke at all — only commendation, an open door, and a sure reward.
blocks.es_reference: Cristo promete vindicar a Filadelfia delante de sus enemigos, haciendo que los de "la sinagoga de Satanás" vengan y se postren a sus pies y sepan que él los ha amado (Apocalipsis 3:9). Luego viene una promesa preciosa: "Por cuanto has guardado la palabra de mi paciencia, yo también te guardaré de la hora de la prueba que ha de venir sobre todo el mundo" (Apocalipsis 3:10). Los cristianos han entendido "te guardaré de la hora de la prueba" de más de una manera — algunos como ser guardados a salvo a través de la prueba, otros como ser guardados fuera de ella por completo — y el curso deja esa pregunta abierta, notando solo la certeza de que Cristo guardará a su pueblo fiel. Añade: "He aquí, yo vengo pronto; retén lo que tienes, para que ninguno tome tu corona" (Apocalipsis 3:11). Al que vence le promete hacerlo "columna en el templo de mi Dios," permanente y seguro, inscrito con el nombre de Dios, el nombre de la ciudad de Dios, la nueva Jerusalén, y el nombre nuevo de Cristo mismo (Apocalipsis 3:12). Como Esmirna, Filadelfia no recibe reprensión alguna — solo elogio, una puerta abierta, y un galardón seguro.

blocks.en: Laodicea: Neither Cold Nor Hot
blocks.es_reference: Laodicea: Ni Frío Ni Caliente

blocks.en: To Laodicea the letter comes from "the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness, the Beginning of the creation of God" (Revelation 3:14), the One whose word is utterly reliable. And the word He speaks is severe, for Laodicea is the only one of the seven churches that receives no commendation at all. One writer has called these verses an autopsy of a dead church. "I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. I could wish you were cold or hot. So then, because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will vomit you out of My mouth" (Revelation 3:15-16). The word cold pictures the unconverted person who has never yet been warmed by the gospel; the word hot, in the original, carries the sense of boiling, or "zesty," and pictures the believer on fire for the Lord. Laodicea was neither. Perhaps they had once been hot, but they had cooled into the lukewarm, with no enthusiasm, no urgency, no compassion. The very name Laodicea was understood to mean something like "the rights of the people," and the church had become exactly that, a people thinking of their own rights and preferences rather than how they might serve the Lord. Any church can drift there, wanting singing, sermons, and programs that please itself, when it ought to be asking how its members might better serve Christ. The picture is easy to feel: tea is welcome piping hot and refreshing poured cold over ice, but a cup gone lukewarm is flat and sickening, and the first sip is spit straight back out. Just so, lukewarmness is nauseating to Christ, who says the lukewarm church makes Him want to spew it from His mouth; He would sooner a church be honestly cold than comfortably lukewarm.
blocks.es_reference: A Laodicea la carta viene de "el Amén, el testigo fiel y verdadero, el principio de la creación de Dios" (Apocalipsis 3:14), aquel cuya palabra es totalmente confiable. Y la palabra que habla es severa, pues Laodicea es la única de las siete iglesias que no recibe elogio alguno. Alguien ha llamado a estos versículos una autopsia de una iglesia muerta. "Yo conozco tus obras, que ni eres frío ni caliente. ¡Ojalá fueses frío o caliente! Mas porque eres tibio, y no frío ni caliente, te vomitaré de mi boca" (Apocalipsis 3:15-16). La palabra frío retrata a la persona no convertida que nunca ha sido calentada por el evangelio; la palabra caliente, en el original, lleva el sentido de hervir, y retrata al creyente encendido para el Señor. Laodicea no era ninguno. Quizás una vez habían sido calientes, pero se habían enfriado hasta volverse tibios, sin entusiasmo, sin urgencia, sin compasión. El nombre mismo de Laodicea se entendía como algo así como "los derechos del pueblo," y la iglesia se había vuelto exactamente eso, un pueblo que pensaba en sus propios derechos y preferencias en vez de cómo podría servir al Señor. Cualquier iglesia puede derivar allí, queriendo el canto, los sermones y los programas que le agradan a sí misma, cuando debería estar preguntando cómo sus miembros podrían servir mejor a Cristo. La imagen es fácil de sentir: el té se recibe bien muy caliente y refresca servido frío con hielo, pero una taza que se ha entibiado es desabrida y repugnante, y el primer sorbo se escupe de inmediato. Así también la tibieza le da náuseas a Cristo, quien dice que la iglesia tibia le da ganas de vomitarla de su boca; preferiría que una iglesia fuese honestamente fría a cómodamente tibia.

blocks.en: Laodicea: The Lukewarm Heart
blocks.es_reference: Laodicea: El Corazón Tibio

blocks.en: The deepest danger of lukewarmness is that it does not know itself. "You say, 'I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing'—and do not know that you are wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17). They felt prosperous and self-sufficient; Christ saw spiritual poverty and shame. Several marks expose the lukewarm heart. First, it seeks first the things of this world. Laodicea had reversed the Lord's command to seek first the kingdom, and their pride was in what they had acquired. One man dreamed he came to heaven's gate clutching his stocks and his gold, only to be told that in that city gold is merely paving and what is treasured there is souls — and many will arrive with full hands and empty lives. Second, the lukewarm heart grows indifferent to sin. A society slowly loses its capacity to be shocked, until what once scandalized becomes ordinary entertainment, and the church ceases to be troubled by sin in itself or in others. A man stealing potatoes by night looked carefully in every direction but one; as his son reminded him, he had forgotten to look up, and an age of spiritual forgetfulness forgets that all must stand before the judgment seat. Third, the lukewarm heart has no interest in service. Laodicea was doing nothing for God. Christians tend to cool, beginning with fire and slowly growing cold, yet the one who stays near Christ stays near the flame. Like relief trucks that cannot reach starving people because the bridge has collapsed, a believer who will not carry the gospel leaves others stranded, and one trembles to imagine a soul in eternity asking, "Why did you never tell me?" Fourth, the lukewarm heart has no assurance. Scripture says we know that we know Him by keeping His commandments (1 John 2:3) — not by having walked an aisle, been baptized, or had believing parents, but by a life of obedience. The lukewarm man lacks assurance because he knows he is not walking in obedience.
blocks.es_reference: El peligro más profundo de la tibieza es que no se conoce a sí misma. "Porque tú dices: Yo soy rico, y estoy enriquecido, y no tengo necesidad de ninguna cosa; y no conoces que tú eres un desventurado y miserable y pobre y ciego y desnudo" (Apocalipsis 3:17). Se sentían prósperos y autosuficientes; Cristo veía pobreza espiritual y vergüenza. Varias marcas exponen el corazón tibio. Primera, busca primero las cosas de este mundo. Laodicea había invertido el mandato del Señor de buscar primero el reino, y su orgullo estaba en lo que había adquirido. Un hombre soñó que llegaba a la puerta del cielo aferrando sus acciones y su oro, solo para que le dijeran que en aquella ciudad el oro es mero pavimento y lo que se atesora allí son las almas — y muchos llegarán con las manos llenas y la vida vacía. Segunda, el corazón tibio se vuelve indiferente al pecado. Una sociedad pierde lentamente su capacidad de escandalizarse, hasta que lo que una vez escandalizaba se vuelve entretenimiento ordinario, y la iglesia deja de inquietarse por el pecado en sí misma o en otros. Un hombre que robaba papas de noche miró con cuidado en toda dirección menos una; como le recordó su hijo, había olvidado mirar hacia arriba, y una época de olvido espiritual olvida que todos hemos de comparecer ante el tribunal. Tercera, el corazón tibio no tiene interés en el servicio. Laodicea no hacía nada para Dios. Los cristianos tienden a enfriarse, comenzando con fuego y poco a poco volviéndose fríos, pero el que se queda cerca de Cristo se queda cerca de la llama. Como camiones de auxilio que no pueden llegar a la gente hambrienta porque el puente se ha derrumbado, un creyente que no lleva el evangelio deja a otros varados, y uno tiembla al imaginar a un alma en la eternidad preguntando: "¿Por qué nunca me lo dijiste?" Cuarta, el corazón tibio no tiene seguridad. La Escritura dice que sabemos que le conocemos guardando sus mandamientos (1 Juan 2:3) — no por haber caminado un pasillo, sido bautizados, o tenido padres creyentes, sino por una vida de obediencia. El hombre tibio carece de seguridad porque sabe que no anda en obediencia.

blocks.en: Laodicea: The Gold, the Knock, and the Throne
blocks.es_reference: Laodicea: El Oro, el Llamado, y el Trono

blocks.en: Yet even to this church Christ comes not only with rebuke but with remedy. "I counsel you to buy from Me gold refined in the fire, that you may be rich; and white garments, that you may be clothed... and anoint your eyes with eye salve, that you may see" (Revelation 3:18). For their imagined wealth He offers true riches; for their nakedness, white garments; for their blindness, sight. And He frames the whole rebuke in love: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten. Therefore be zealous and repent" (Revelation 3:19). His sharp words are not the voice of an enemy but of a Lord who loves them too much to leave them as they are. Then comes one of the tenderest verses in all Scripture: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me" (Revelation 3:20). A famous painting, The Light of the World by Holman Hunt, shows Christ knocking at a door with no latch on the outside, a door that can be opened only from within. To a self-satisfied church the living Lord stands outside, patiently knocking, asking to be let back in. And to the one who opens, the one who overcomes, He gives the highest promise of all the seven: "To him who overcomes I will grant to sit with Me on My throne, as I also overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne" (Revelation 3:21). The letters to all seven churches end as they began, with the same call: "He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches" (Revelation 3:22). Across both chapters the message is one — Christ knows His churches, calls them to repent, and reserves His richest promises for the one who hears His voice and overcomes.
blocks.es_reference: Sin embargo, aun a esta iglesia Cristo viene no solo con reprensión sino con remedio. "Yo te aconsejo que de mí compres oro refinado en fuego, para que seas rico; y vestiduras blancas, para que te vistas... y unge tus ojos con colirio, para que veas" (Apocalipsis 3:18). Por su riqueza imaginada él ofrece riquezas verdaderas; por su desnudez, vestiduras blancas; por su ceguera, vista. Y enmarca toda la reprensión en amor: "Yo reprendo y castigo a todos los que amo; sé pues celoso, y arrepiéntete" (Apocalipsis 3:19). Sus palabras agudas no son la voz de un enemigo sino de un Señor que los ama demasiado para dejarlos como están. Luego viene uno de los versículos más tiernos de toda la Escritura: "He aquí, yo estoy a la puerta y llamo; si alguno oye mi voz y abre la puerta, entraré a él, y cenaré con él, y él conmigo" (Apocalipsis 3:20). Una pintura famosa, La Luz del Mundo de Holman Hunt, muestra a Cristo llamando a una puerta sin pestillo por fuera, una puerta que solo puede abrirse desde dentro. A una iglesia satisfecha de sí misma el Señor viviente está afuera, llamando pacientemente, pidiendo que lo dejen entrar de nuevo. Y al que abre, al que vence, le da la promesa más alta de las siete: "Al que venciere, yo le daré que se siente conmigo en mi trono; así como yo he vencido, y me he sentado con mi Padre en su trono" (Apocalipsis 3:21). Las cartas a las siete iglesias terminan como comenzaron, con el mismo llamado: "El que tiene oído, oiga lo que el Espíritu dice a las iglesias" (Apocalipsis 3:22). A través de ambos capítulos el mensaje es uno — Cristo conoce a sus iglesias, las llama a arrepentirse, y reserva sus promesas más ricas para el que oye su voz y vence.

blocks.en: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me." — Revelation 3:20 (NKJV)

mc.stem: Christ introduces Himself to Sardis as having the seven Spirits of God and:
options: Eyes like a flame of fire
mc.why: To Sardis: He who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars (3:1).

mc.stem: Sardis had a reputation, "a name," that it was alive, but Christ declared it was in fact:
mc.why: "You have a name that you are alive, but you are dead" (3:1).

mc.stem: Christ's command to Sardis was to be watchful and to:
mc.why: "Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain" (3:2).

mc.stem: If Sardis would not watch, Christ warned that He would come upon them:
options: Like a thief, at an unexpected hour
mc.why: He would come like a thief, at an unknown hour (3:3).

mc.stem: Christ noted a few in Sardis who were worthy because they had not:
mc.why: A few had not defiled their garments and would walk with Him in white (3:4).

mc.stem: To the one who overcomes at Sardis, Christ promises white garments and that his name will not be:
options: Blotted out of the Book of Life
mc.why: His name will not be blotted out of the Book of Life (3:5).

mc.stem: Christ introduces Himself to Philadelphia as holy, true, and having:
options: A book sealed with seven seals
mc.why: He is holy and true and holds the key of David (3:7).

mc.stem: Before Philadelphia Christ set something that no one can shut, namely:
mc.why: "I have set before you an open door, and no one can shut it" (3:8).

mc.stem: Though it had little strength, Philadelphia had kept Christ's word and had not:
mc.why: They kept His word and did not deny His name (3:8).

mc.stem: Christ promised to keep Philadelphia from:
options: The hour of trial coming upon the whole world
mc.why: He will keep them from the hour of trial that comes on the world (3:10).

mc.stem: To the one who overcomes at Philadelphia, Christ promises to make him:
options: A pillar in the temple of God
mc.why: The overcomer becomes a pillar in the temple of God (3:12).

mc.stem: Like Smyrna, the church at Philadelphia received from Christ:
mc.why: Philadelphia (with Smyrna) receives no rebuke (3:7-13).

mc.stem: Christ introduces Himself to Laodicea as the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness, and:
options: The Beginning of the creation of God
mc.why: To Laodicea: the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness, the Beginning of God's creation (3:14).

mc.stem: The central problem with the church at Laodicea was that they were:
mc.why: They were lukewarm, neither cold nor hot (3:15-16).

mc.stem: Because Laodicea was lukewarm, Christ said He would:
options: Vomit them out of His mouth
mc.why: "Because you are lukewarm... I will vomit you out of My mouth" (3:16).

mc.stem: Laodicea said, "I am rich... and have need of nothing," but Christ said they were:
options: Wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked
mc.why: In truth they were wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked (3:17).

mc.stem: Christ counseled Laodicea to buy from Him gold refined in fire, white garments, and:
options: Eye salve, that they might see
mc.why: Gold, white garments, and eye salve to anoint their eyes that they may see (3:18).

mc.stem: When Christ says, "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten," He teaches that His rebuke springs from:
mc.why: Christ's rebuke and chastening flow from His love (3:19).

mc.stem: In Revelation 3:20 Christ pictures Himself as:
options: Seated on a great white throne
Standing at the door and knocking
mc.why: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock" (3:20).

mc.stem: To the one who overcomes at Laodicea, Christ gives the highest promise of all seven, namely to:
options: Sit with Him on His throne
Eat of the tree of life
mc.why: "To him who overcomes I will grant to sit with Me on My throne" (3:21).

To Philadelphia, which had only a little strength, Christ says, "I have set before you an open ____, and no one can shut it."
Christ promises to make the overcomer at Philadelphia "a ____ in the temple of My God," permanent and secure.
Because Laodicea is ____, neither cold nor hot, Christ says He will vomit it out of His mouth.
The name Laodicea was understood to mean something like "the ____ of the people."
For Laodicea's blindness Christ counsels them to anoint their eyes with ____, that they may see.
To the self-satisfied church Christ says, "Behold, I stand at the door and ____."

sa.prompt: How does Christ describe the church at Sardis, and what is the danger of "a name that you are alive, but you are dead"?
sa.model: To Sardis Christ comes as the One who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars, and His verdict is sobering: you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead. Sardis had a reputation; to those around it the church looked alive, busy, and respected. But the eyes that search the lampstands saw past the reputation to the truth, that inwardly the church was dead. The danger this exposes is that a congregation can keep its name, its buildings, and its routines long after the life has gone out of it, becoming in effect a morgue, orderly and quiet yet a place of the dead. Christ does not flatter such a church but tells it the truth, and then calls it to be watchful, to strengthen what remains, to remember how it first received the gospel, and to repent, warning that otherwise He will come upon it like a thief at an unexpected hour.

sa.prompt: What does Christ command Sardis to do, and what hope remains for the faithful few?
sa.model: Christ commands Sardis to wake up: be watchful, and strengthen the things that remain and are ready to die. They are to remember how they had received and heard the gospel, to hold it fast, and to repent, for if they will not watch He will come like a thief. Yet hope remains, because even in a dying church the Lord knows every faithful soul. He says there are a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments, and they shall walk with Him in white, for they are worthy. This leads to the promise to the overcomer: he will be clothed in white garments, his name will not be blotted out of the Book of Life, and Christ will confess his name before the Father and the angels. So the dead church is called to wake, while the faithful within it are assured that Christ knows them by name and will own them at the last.

sa.prompt: Describe the church at Philadelphia and the meaning of the open door Christ set before it.
sa.model: Philadelphia receives its letter from the One who is holy and true and holds the key of David, the authority to open and shut the door of the kingdom, so that what He opens no power can shut. To this church He says He has set before it an open door that no one can shut, because, though it has only a little strength, it has kept His word and has not denied His name. Philadelphia was not a powerful church, yet it had been faithful in the two things that matter most, keeping Christ's word and confessing His name. The open door is both an opportunity for witness and service and an entrance into His kingdom that no enemy can close. The lesson is that Christ honors faithfulness rather than strength, and a small, weak church that holds fast His word and refuses to deny His name lacks nothing it truly needs, for the Lord Himself has opened the way before it.

sa.prompt: What does Christ promise the faithful at Philadelphia, including the overcomer's reward?
sa.model: To Philadelphia Christ makes several promises. He will vindicate them before their enemies, making those of the synagogue of Satan come and bow at their feet and know that He has loved them. Because they kept His command to persevere, He will keep them from the hour of trial that is to come upon the whole world; Christians have understood this keeping either as protection through the trial or as removal from it, and the lesson leaves the question open. He tells them He is coming quickly and urges them to hold fast what they have so that no one takes their crown. And to the one who overcomes He promises to make him a pillar in the temple of God, permanent and secure, inscribed with the name of God, the name of the city of God, the New Jerusalem, and Christ's own new name. Like Smyrna, Philadelphia receives no rebuke, only commendation, an open door, and a sure reward.

sa.prompt: Explain what it means that Laodicea was "lukewarm," including the picture of cold, hot, and lukewarm.
sa.model: Laodicea was the only one of the seven churches to receive no commendation, and one writer has called Christ's words to it an autopsy of a dead church. Christ says they are neither cold nor hot, and because they are lukewarm He will vomit them out of His mouth. The word cold pictures the unconverted person who has never been warmed by the gospel; the word hot carries the sense of boiling, picturing a believer on fire for the Lord. Laodicea was neither. Perhaps they had once been hot, but they had cooled into the lukewarm, with no enthusiasm, no urgency, and no compassion. Their very name was understood to mean the rights of the people, and the church had become a people thinking of their own rights and preferences rather than how they might serve the Lord. Lukewarmness is nauseating to Christ, who would rather a church be honestly cold than comfortably lukewarm, and so He calls them to be zealous and to repent.

sa.prompt: What did Laodicea believe about itself, and what did Christ say was the truth?
sa.model: The deepest danger of Laodicea's lukewarmness was that it did not know itself. The church said, I am rich, have become wealthy, and have need of nothing. They felt prosperous and entirely self-sufficient, confident that they lacked nothing. But Christ told them the truth they could not see: they did not know that they were wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. What they counted as wealth was spiritual poverty; what they thought was clothing left them naked; what they took for sight was blindness. This is the great deception of the lukewarm heart, that it measures itself by outward prosperity and feels no need, while in the eyes of Christ it is bankrupt and ashamed. The gap between their estimate of themselves and Christ's estimate of them is the very heart of the rebuke, and it is why He counsels them to buy from Him the true gold, garments, and sight they so desperately lack.

sa.prompt: Describe the marks of the lukewarm heart that this lesson draws out from the letter to Laodicea.
sa.model: The lesson draws several marks of the lukewarm heart from the letter to Laodicea. First, it seeks first the things of this world; Laodicea had reversed the command to seek first the kingdom, taking pride in what it had acquired, though one cannot serve both God and money. Second, it grows indifferent to sin; a society loses its capacity to be shocked until sin becomes ordinary, and the church stops being troubled by it, like a man so forgetful of God that he forgets to look up. Third, it has no interest in service; Laodicea was doing nothing for God, and Christians tend to cool from their first fire, though the one who stays near Christ stays near the flame and carries the gospel to others. Fourth, it has no assurance; Scripture says we know that we know Him by keeping His commandments, not by an aisle walked or a baptism received, so the lukewarm man lacks assurance because he knows he is not walking in obedience.

sa.prompt: What is Christ's counsel and remedy to Laodicea (the gold, the garments, and the salve)?
sa.model: Even to this lukewarm church Christ comes not only with rebuke but with remedy, counseling them to buy from Him three things that answer their three needs. He offers gold refined in the fire, so that the church that thought it was rich may become truly rich toward God. He offers white garments, so that the church it believed was clothed may cover the shame of its nakedness. And He offers eye salve to anoint their eyes, so that the church that thought it could see may receive sight for its blindness. Each remedy must be bought from Christ Himself, which means received from Him by faith, for they cannot supply it on their own. The counsel exposes how empty their imagined wealth was and how full His provision is. It is the language of grace, not of rejection, for the same Lord who rebukes them stands ready to give them the true riches, covering, and sight they lack.

sa.prompt: Explain Revelation 3:19-20: Christ's rebuke, His knock at the door, and what they reveal about His love.
sa.model: Revelation 3:19-20 turns the severe letter toward grace. Christ says, As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten; therefore be zealous and repent. His sharp words are not the voice of an enemy but of a Lord who loves them, for love that is real will rebuke and chasten rather than leave a person in ruin. Then comes one of the tenderest verses in Scripture: Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears My voice and opens the door, He will come in and dine with him. A famous painting shows Christ knocking at a door that has no handle on the outside, a door that can be opened only from within. The picture is striking: to a self-satisfied church the living Lord stands outside, patiently knocking, asking to be let back in. Together these verses reveal that the whole rebuke flows from love, and that Christ does not force His way in but waits for the heart that will hear His voice and open the door.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central lesson of Unit 4: what do the letters to Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea teach the church?
sa.model: The central lesson of Unit 4 is that the risen Christ knows each church exactly as it is and calls each according to its need. To Sardis, a dead church with a living reputation, He says wake up, strengthen what remains, and repent, while assuring the faithful few that He knows them by name. To Philadelphia, a weak but faithful church, He gives no rebuke at all, only an open door that no one can shut, because it kept His word and did not deny His name. To Laodicea, a lukewarm and self-satisfied church, He speaks His sharpest words, exposing its imagined wealth, counseling it to buy true gold and garments and sight, and standing at the door to knock. Across all three the pattern holds: Christ tells the truth in love, calls every church to repent, and reserves His richest promises, from the Book of Life to a place on His own throne, for the one who hears His voice and overcomes.
